newsitem.title: USA: Study finds Alzheimer's disease tied to strokes.
newsitem.headline: Study finds Alzheimer's disease tied to strokes.

text.p: In a development described as encouraging for the future treatment of Alzheimer's disease, researchers reported Tuesday that small strokes may determine the onset and severity of the mentally crippling disease.

The report, from the University of Kentucky, said that even one or two small strokes in strategic regions of the brain can dramatically increase the risk of developing the overt symptoms of the disease and their severity once developed.
The finding was based on a study of Roman Catholic nuns whose health was traced for a number of years.

Autopsies found that 61 of the women had brain lesions that indicated the presence of Alzheimer's disease. In that group, however, those who had also suffered strokes were more likely to have developed the dementia that marks the worst stages of the disease, the study said.

"This study provides some hope that treatments and prevention strategies currently used for stroke and other cerebrovascular disease, such as atherosclerosis, may prove helpful in treating some people with Alzheimer's disease," said Zaven Khachaturian, an expert on the disease.

"This is very encouraging news," he added in a statement. Khachaturian is the director of the Ronald and Nancy Reagan Research Insitutue, an arm of the Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders Association. The former president suffers from the disease.
The Kentucky study was published, along with several other reports on the disease, in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.

In one of them, researchers at Columbia University said they had worked out a formula that can predict how long Alzheimer's victims are likely to live before they require admission to a nursing home or reach the end stage of the disease.
The formula is based on a number of variables including age, sex and loss of mental ability.
